newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE-Surviving with a smile in Moscow on $175 a month.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Surviving with a smile in Moscow on $175 a month.

text.p: Sofia Gorelik surveyed the well-stocked food store but found just one item she could afford, a pack of frozen Polish vegetables for a dollar.
A teacher of seven- and eight-year olds in southern Moscow, 28-year-old Gorelik makes the average Russian wage, about $175 a month, and she shops with great care to make ends meet.
"Russians can survive on almost nothing," she said. "I live okay, but on the other hand there are many things I'd like to buy or do that I can't anymore."
The freeing of prices in 1992 has transformed Moscow into one of the world's most expensive cities, according to many surveys.
A good traditional fur hat can cost $150, a beer in a chic nightclub $20 after a $75 entrance fee, U.S.-made jeans $100, a swim in an heated outdoor pool of uncertain cleanliness $10.

Yet salaries for the majority of Russians lag far behind. For those like Gorelik earning a typical pay cheque, the key to survival is avoiding these and many other budget-busters much as a captain steers clear of rocks in a shallow bay.
SOFIA'S CHOICES
Gorelik admits she is better off than many teachers, three million of whom went on strike in January because they had not been paid for months.
Her state salary is doubled by parental donations which the school started collecting last year to boost its meagre budget.
She takes home a total of a million roubles a month ($175), spending a little less than half on food, and $17-$35 on transport.
She lives with her student brother and her factory worker parents in a small two bedroomed flat in a Moscow suburb -- an hour from work on a battered suburban train.
"My father is a difficult person and things can get tense at home," she said. "He loves a strict regime and I'm disorganised."

Living at home means savings on the rent, but Gorelik says she often bails out her parents when their own wages come in late. She helped out in 1994 as well when her father lost much of his savings when a get-rich-quick pyramid scheme crashed.
Anything left over from food and transport Gorelik spends, carefully, for herself.

An attractive woman who admits her clothes are well-worn and often drab, Gorelik shops for replacements just once a year. She uses little make-up because her favorite Western-made cosmetics are too expensive.

She thinks twice before buying a newspaper, magazine or ice cream and goes to restaurants only if someone else invites her. She remembers a recent visit to the Bolshoi Theatre as an incredible splurge: $8 for one of the worst seats in the house.
THE SECRET CORNERS OF THE RUSSIAN ECONOMY

For many Russians, their lifestyle is not as bleak as their official pay would suggest, as freelance work is a hidden engine of the Russian economy. Gorelik makes crafts such as glass beads to sell, and tutors a friend's child for $5 an hour.
Another staple of Russian life hidden from official data is the dacha garden plot. Many summer family meals come from the plot, and the preserved bounty lasts until winter.
Then there is the Soviet-era tradition of outsmarting the government. For Gorelik this means asking her brother to buy a monthly metro pass at a student price, saving her about $8.
"I cheat the government," she says. "I still look like a student perhaps, and the control is not very strong."
Tough times have cheated Gorelik in their own way, taking a toll in less measurable ways such as her relationships.
As Moscow restaurants cast off the Soviet-era staple of loud pop bands during dinner, her once well-paid boyfriend, a bass guitarist, found it hard to earn a living, and romance soured.
"He became very pessimistic because he didn't have any work," she said. Finally he left for Thailand where he found work in a resort.
THE LURE OF THE CHILDREN
Her workplace, a three-storey grey building called Middle School 578 camouflaged amid similiar drab Soviet-era blocks, appears an unlikely lure for a dedicated worker.
But with its cheery drawings on the wall and young pupils keen to answer her questions, Gorelik considers the school a second home.
"She is one of the best," said Yelena Nartova, whose daughter is in Gorelik's class. "Those teachers are very rare because the prestige of the profession is so low."

As a young energetic woman with nine years teaching experience, Gorelik could probably find a better-paying job -- an opportunity beyond the reach of many middle-aged Russians living in one-factory towns. But she says she would sooner stay.

"At the school, only those who can't do anything else -- the older teachers -- and those who love working here are left," she said. "I've had offers to go elsewhere but I cannot because I love the children and teaching."
But even if she lives modestly, Gorelik says she enjoys life. "Of course, one wants to live better, but I am happy because I have many good friends," she said.
